title: Redwood discovery with Boreal Intel - cost discussion
summary: Discovery focused on unit economics for inference. Boreal uses transformer assistant features for analytics; they need predictable cost under a $50k/month token budget. Discussed per-token billing, effectiveness of batching and KV/prefix caching, and when Dedicated or Private makes sense for predictable unit cost. Action: send pricing matrix, recommended batching config, and plan for a short benchmark on sample workload.
transcript:
00:00 Sarah (Redwood): Hey everyone thanks for joining. we got about 40 minutes, quick intros.
00:06 Maya (Boreal): Maya here, CTO, thanks. Tariq, Evan, Lina also with me.
00:11 Sarah: Great, before we dive Daniel who's our SE will take the deep cost bit.
00:15 Daniel (Redwood): Hey all. quick overview: Redwood offers hosted API, Dedicated reserved pools, and Private (VPC / on prem). main levers for cost are model choice, batching, and caching (prefix + KV). also quantization/compute selection.
00:30 Tariq (Boreal): Our workload is analytics assistant for internal ops, about 10M tokens / month today, expect 3x growth next year. budget approximately 50k USD per month target.
00:42 Daniel: ok that's helpful. are those 10M tokens input only or in/out?
00:45 Tariq: approx in+out. average prompt length 300 tokens, responses around 1500 on long explainers but 70% are shorter.
00:58 Sarah: so burstiness is a factor? do you have steady QPS or spikes?
01:02 Evan (Boreal): spikes around morning reports and ad-hoc queries, 300-400 rps for short times, sustained 20-40 rps otherwise.
01:12 Daniel: good. so cost math: hosted per-token pricing varies by model, e.g. a 70B open model at nominal hosted rate might be X per 1k tokens (we call out in the pricing sheet). but important: batching can reduce per-token compute by grouping requests into larger batches on the GPU. continuous batching gives you throughput wins, but trades off a few ms latency.
01:34 Maya: quantify that for us — how much can batching reduce unit cost?
01:38 Daniel: ballpark — for throughput-optimized workloads we see 20-50% per-token cost reduction from batching + KV caching depending on seq length. for traces with long outputs, caching helps if you have repeat prefixes or system prompts. prefix caching can cut repeated prompt costs dramatically.
01:54 Lina (Finance): we need predictable unit cost to forecast. hosted variable pricing is a bit noisy for us. how does Dedicated change that?
02:02 Daniel: Dedicated gives you reserved GPU pools and you pay committed capacity (monthly); unit cost on committed capacity is lower and more predictable because you control batch sizing and you avoid per-request overhead. we can show committed throughput numbers per GPU type.
02:16 Tariq: what's the break-even in tokens for Dedicated vs Hosted?
02:19 Daniel: depends — if you're running steady 100M tokens/month, Dedicated usually starts to make sense. with your growth curve (30M soon) you may be near the cusp. but KV caching and smarter batching on hosted can push Hosted to be economical in the short term.
02:37 Maya: and Private? we have regulatory customers that want VPC with customer KMS and audit logs.
02:44 Daniel: Private gives full control — but you take on infra ops. unit cost depends on your infra contracts and utilization. Redwood's pricing for Private is a platform fee plus either a per-token metered or capacity-based plan. many customers run Private when they need KMS/HSM, region residency, or consistent compliance.
02:59 Evan: for dedicated pricing, do we still get Redwood's optimizations like continuous batching and kernel choices?
03:04 Daniel: yes — same serving runtime. Dedicated just restricts the pool to you.
03:08 Tariq: we worry about cold-starts and tail latency if we rely on batching. our SLAs are 95th perc require ~300ms for short queries.
03:17 Daniel: ok that matters. continuous batching is latency-aware; you can set latency SLOs and it will batch within that window. also you can set a mixed fleet: a fraction on dedicated low-latency nodes and some on throughput nodes to save cost.
03:33 Maya: can you share a worked example? say model A hosted price is 0.002 USD per 1k tokens — is that realistic?
03:41 Daniel: numbers vary; for example purposes: hosted model A 0.002 /1k, model B (bigger) 0.01 /1k. with 30M tokens: at 0.002 it's $60/month? (note: we messed a decimal) — sorry let me re-run verbally: 30M tokens at 0.002 per 1k tokens = 30,000 * 0.002 = $60, yes but in practice a 0.002 is for embeddings or tiny cheaper models; generation model rates often in the 0.5 to 5 per 1k tokens in some vendors — Redwood's public pricing sheet will have accurate rates. Important thing is percent reductions from batching/caching.
04:13 Lina: that example makes me double-check math. we prefer per-API call forecasting. do you provide token forecasting tools in console?
04:20 Daniel: yes console shows token breakdown by route/model and peak projections; we can export. also you can set per-team quotas.
04:29 Tariq: about caching: our agent prompts include long system messages and user context that repeats. how effective is prefix caching for those?
04:36 Daniel: very effective — if your system prompt + user context repeats 60% of the time, you can save most of the forward pass compute for those prefixes. for generative outputs you still pay for the decode tokens. you'd see up to 40-70% reduction on the input side for repeated prefixes.
04:52 Maya: what's the operational effort to enable KV cache across requests?
04:56 Daniel: it's built-in — clients can provide cache keys or we can auto-derive from conversation history. there are SDK hooks, you'd need to decide TTLs and privacy rules (e.g., not caching PII).
05:08 Evan: from infra side, if we go Dedicated, what's scaling model? do you autoscale GPUs?
05:13 Daniel: Dedicated supports autoscaling policies: scheduled, metric-driven (latency/queue), and burst pools. you set min/max and we orchestrate. with Private you manage nodes but we provide recommended configs.
05:24 Maya: procurement will want a clear TCO comparison. can you produce a side-by-side: Hosted per-token with expected effective discount from batching/caching; Dedicated committed rate with expected utilization assumptions; Private TCO baseline.
05:36 Sarah: yes we'll send a pricing matrix and a worked TCO with a couple utilization scenarios. we'll include assumptions so you can plug in your numbers.
05:43 Lina: about bill smoothing — do you allow committed spend to be applied to Hosted overages?
05:47 Daniel: there are flexible billing options: committed credits can be used for hosted overages and we can craft a hybrid.
05:54 Tariq: timeline: we want a short pilot to validate unit costs on our real prompts. what's a minimum pilot?
05:59 Daniel: we recommend a 2-week bench with 1-2M tokens of representative traffic; we can run it on Hosted with optional Dedicated mirrors. we'll instrument cost-per-token, latency distribution, and cache hit rates.
06:12 Maya: ok excellent. what about security: SOC2, SSO, KMS, audit logs?
06:17 Sarah: Redwood has SOC 2 and ISO attestation, SAML SSO, RBAC, customer KMS integration for Private and Dedicated options, and full audit logs in Console. we'll attach the security pack.
06:28 Evan: any vendor lock-in concerns? we prefer portability. if we start Hosted and later bring Private, migration path?
06:33 Daniel: same API and model versions across deployments, model pinning, and rollout policies make migration straightforward.
06:41 Tariq: competitors — we evaluated OpenAI and Anthropic; cost was higher per token and less control. we also looked at self-hosting but infra ops was heavy.
06:51 Sarah: understood. next steps?
06:53 Sarah: recap: we'll send pricing matrix, security docs, and a recommended pilot plan + benchmark script. we'll schedule a pilot kickoff after you sign the SOW if that's the path.
07:03 Lina: procurement wants a statement of work and pilot SOW, + data processing addendum.
07:08 Sarah: we'll include those.
07:10 Maya: ok thanks everyone.
07:12 Daniel: thanks, we'll follow up in email with attachments and a proposed pilot start date.
07:17 [end of recording]
